analysis.one_liner: Would expand what inventions qualify for patents by wiping out most court-created limits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in September 2024 and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the core patent law to eliminate the judge-made exceptions that courts have used for years to deny patents on things like abstract ideas, natural phenomena, and plain business methods. It would make software, financial and business processes that run on a machine, purified natural materials, and isolated human genes eligible for patents again, while keeping narrow bans on pure math formulas, mental processes, and business methods a person can perform by hand. It was introduced in September 2024, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and never received any further action before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patent-holding industries gain the most: brand-name drug and biotech companies (which could re-patent isolated genes, purified natural materials, and diagnostic methods), technology firms with large patent portfolios, and firms whose business is asserting or licensing patents. Patent lawyers and litigation-heavy business models also gain from a larger pool of enforceable patents.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patent-holding drug, biotech, and tech companies

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that all judicial exceptions to patent eligibility are eliminated, restoring eligibility to inventions that courts have increasingly ruled unpatentable in recent decades.

It redefines unmodified genes and natural materials so that a gene or material that is merely 'isolated, purified, enriched, or otherwise altered by human activity' counts as modified and can be patented — reopening claims of the kind courts struck down in the Myriad Genetics case over human gene patents.

A business, financial, or social process is patentable if it cannot 'practically be performed without the use of a machine or manufacture,' which reopens broad categories of software-implemented methods, while adding 'do it on a computer' to an otherwise human process stays ineligible.

It requires that eligibility be judged without regard to whether claim elements are 'known, conventional, routine, or naturally occurring,' making it easier to obtain and defend patents that combine familiar pieces.

analysis.who_pays: Broader patents raise costs that land on ordinary people indirectly: owners of gene and diagnostic-method patents can charge more for genetic tests, more software and business-method patents mean more infringement suits and licensing demands whose costs get passed through prices, and generic competition and follow-on research can be slowed by thicker patent thickets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers, small firms facing more patent suits

drawbacks.text: By making isolated human genes and purified natural materials patentable, the bill would let companies claim exclusive rights over substances that exist in nature, which courts previously rejected as a roadblock to genetic testing and medical research.

Widening eligibility for software and business processes that run on a machine invites more patents of the kind that historically fueled demand letters and infringement suits against small businesses, with the bill only excluding processes a human could perform unaided.

Supporters would answer that courts had drifted into denying patents on real, useful inventions — the bill's own findings say judges created exceptions that 'rendered an increasing number of inventions ineligible' — and that clearer rules would help inventors and investors; the bill does retain exclusions for pure formulas, mental processes, and hand-performed business methods, so it is not a blanket giveaway.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a genuine argument that current eligibility law is confusing and too restrictive, and the bill would help some legitimate inventors, particularly in software and diagnostics. But its largest concrete effects run to companies that already hold large patent portfolios — restoring patents on isolated genes and purified natural materials and reopening machine-implemented business methods — and the costs (higher diagnostic and drug prices, more litigation) would be diffuse and borne by the public. On balance it is designed around the needs of patent-intensive industries more than of consumers or small firms.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Kevin Kiley introduced the Patent Eligibility Restoration Act of 2024 in the House on September 6, 2024, with Rep. Scott Peters as the other initial sponsor.
The bill's single action after introduction was a referral to the House Committee on the Judiciary on September 6, 2024.
No further action — no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held, which favors everyone who benefits from today's narrower patent rules: companies and patients who rely on affordable genetic testing, generic and follow-on competitors, and the many small businesses that would have faced a larger pool of software and business-method patents. Patent-holding industries gained nothing from this Congress, though the same proposal can be reintroduced at any time.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firms spared a broader patent regime

for.name: Rep. Scott Peters
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's one cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; the record shows no committee action after the referral, and the bill died with the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a bipartisan two-member pair — a Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor (1 of 216 House Democrats) — and never reached a vote, so no party bloc ever took a recorded position.

industries.note: The bill would create a much larger pool of enforceable patents — especially machine-implemented business and software processes — the raw material of licensing demands and infringement suits, whose costs flow to consumers and small firms.

By treating isolated genes and purified natural materials as 'modified' and patentable, the bill would restore exclusive claims of the kind courts struck down, supporting higher prices for genetic tests and slowing competing diagnostics and research.

Firms with large patent portfolios would see their assets strengthen and could patent more machine-implemented methods, but they would also face more infringement exposure and suits under a broader regime.
